groups.label: Vowels & Consonants
rules: English has 5 vowel letters (A, E, I, O, U) representing 20 distinct vowel sounds.
Consonants can be voiced or unvoiced.

groups.label: The Silent-E / Magic-E Rule
groups.definition: A single silent e at the end of a word changes the preceding short vowel into a long vowel that says its letter name
rules: When a word ends in vowel + consonant + silent e (VCE pattern), the final e is unpronounced.
The silent e makes the preceding vowel long (it 'says its name'): a➔/eɪ/, i➔/aɪ/, o➔/əʊ/ or /oʊ/, u➔/juː/ or /uː/.

groups.label: Common Consonant Digraphs
groups.definition: Two consonant letters written together that make a single new consonant sound
rules: SH makes the /ʃ/ sound (shoe, shop, fish).
CH makes the /ʧ/ sound (chair, cheese, watch).
PH makes the /f/ sound (phone, photo, elephant).
WH makes the /w/ sound (white, wheel) or /h/ sound (who, whole).
NG makes the /ŋ/ nasal sound at the end of syllables (sing, long, English).

groups.label: Silent Letters
rules: Silent K in know, knee, knife.
Silent L in listen, talk, walk, half.
Silent W in write, answer, wrong.
Silent B in climb, comb.

groups.label: Pronunciation of -ed and -s Endings
groups.definition: Pronunciation rules for regular past tense -ed and plural/verb -s endings
rules: -ed is pronounced /ɪd/ after /t/ or /d/ (wanted, needed), /t/ after unvoiced sounds (worked, stopped), and /d/ after voiced sounds (played, lived).
-s / -es is pronounced /ɪz/ after sibilants /s, z, ʃ, ʧ, ʤ/ (buses, watches), /s/ after unvoiced sounds (cats, books), and /z/ after voiced sounds (dogs, runs).

groups.label: R-Controlled Vowels
groups.definition: Vowel sounds modified and controlled by a following letter R
rules: When a vowel is followed by R, the letter R changes the vowel sound into a distinct r-controlled vowel.
AR makes /ɑː/ or /ɑːr/ (car, star, park). OR makes /ɔː/ or /ɔːr/ (for, born, short).
ER, IR, UR blend into the same /ɜː/ or /ɜːr/ sound (her, bird, turn). AIR and EAR form vowel glides (fair /feə(r)/, near /nɪə(r)/).

groups.label: Diphthongs & Vowel Duration
groups.definition: Gliding vowel sounds and vowel length before voiced consonants
rules: Diphthongs move from one vowel sound to another within the same syllable (e.g. /eɪ/, /aɪ/, /əʊ/, /aʊ/).
Vowels are pronounced slightly longer before voiced consonants (e.g., bad /bæːd/) than before voiceless ones (e.g., bat /bæt/).

examples.m: Vowel shortening before voiceless /p/ vs lengthening before voiced /b/

groups.label: Glottal Stop & Consonant Assimilation
groups.definition: Glottal replacement of /t/ and sound fusion across word boundaries
rules: Final /t/ is frequently replaced or reinforced by a glottal stop /ʔ/ before consonants or in casual speech (e.g. cat food /kæʔ fʊd/).
Assimilation occurs when sounds blend across word boundaries, such as /t/ + /j/ becoming /ʧ/ (would you ➔ /wʊdʒuː/).

groups.label: Suffix Sound Shifts: -tion, -sion, -cian
groups.definition: Pronunciation of suffix endings -tion, -sion, and -cian as /ʃən/ or /ʒən/
rules: -tion and -cian are pronounced /ʃən/ (nation /ˈneɪʃən/, musician /mjuːˈzɪʃən/).
-sion is pronounced /ʃən/ after consonants (discussion /dɪˈskʌʃən/) and /ʒən/ after vowels (vision /ˈvɪʒən/, decision /dɪˈsɪʒən/).
Stress falls on the syllable immediately preceding these suffixes.

examples.m: -sion pronounced /ʃən/ after consonant vs /ʒən/ after vowel

groups.label: Consonant Clusters & Elision
groups.definition: Complex consonant combinations and sound dropping in natural speech
rules: Consonant clusters occur when two or three consonants appear together without intervening vowels (e.g., /str/, /kts/).
Elision involves dropping weak sounds (like /t/ or /d/) in rapid speech when flanked by other consonants.

examples.t: Next door ➔ /neks dɔːr/, Last night ➔ /lɑːs naɪt/
examples.m: Elision of final /t/ before another consonant

groups.label: Weak Forms & Linking Intrusion
groups.definition: Weak pronunciation of structural words and intrusive linking sounds /r, w, j/
rules: Function words (auxiliaries, prepositions, articles) use weak schwa forms in connected speech, switching to strong forms only for emphasis.
When a word ending in a vowel meets a word beginning with a vowel, intrusive /r/, /w/, or /j/ glides link them smoothly.

examples.t: Fish and chips ➔ /fɪʃ ən ʧɪps/, Must go ➔ /məs ɡəʊ/
Go away ➔ /ɡəʊ ʷ əˈweɪ/, Media event ➔ /ˈmiːdiə ʳ ɪˈvent/

groups.label: Coarticulation & Epenthesis
groups.definition: Advanced articulatory overlap and sound insertion in fluid continuous speech
rules: Coarticulation causes neighboring phonetic segments to adjust their place or manner of articulation simultaneously (e.g., labialization of consonants before /w/ or /uː/).
Epenthesis inserts a brief transitional consonant sound, such as inserting a subtle /p/ between /m/ and /t/ in 'warmth' /wɔːmpθ/.

examples.t: Ten bags ➔ /tem bæɡz/, Good boy ➔ /ɡʊb bɔɪ/

groups.label: Sociolinguistic Phonetic Variation
groups.definition: Phonetic shifts across major regional accents and sociolinguistic registers
rules: Systematic phonetic contrasts separate major international standards, such as rhoticity in General American vs non-rhotic Received Pronunciation.
Vowel shifts like the TRAP-BATH split in Southern British English contrast short /æ/ in 'cat' with broad /ɑː/ in 'dance' and 'path'.

groups.label: Phonological Stylistics & Aesthetics
groups.definition: Articulatory aesthetics, sound symbolism, alliteration, and metrical structures in formal speech
rules: Phonological stylistics analyzes how acoustic properties (euphony, cacophony, sibilance) create emotional texture in literature and public rhetoric.
Metrical cadence in formal English depends on regular stress feet (iambs, trochees, dactyls) balancing spoken energy.

examples.t: Soft sibilance: 'Silently Slipped the Silver Serpent'
Iambic cadence: 'To BE or NOT to BE'
